'''''Rumex salicifolius''''' is a species of flowering perennial plant in the [[Polygonaceae|knotweed family]] known by the common names '''willow dock'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUSA|taxon=Rumex salicifolius|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> and '''willow-leaved dock'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> It is native to much of western North America, and more specifically, in southern and central parts of California, and some parts of Arizona and Nevada.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://beta.floranorthamerica.org/Rumex_salicifolius|title=Rumex salicifolius - FNA|website=beta.floranorthamerica.org|access-date=2019-09-19}}</ref> It can also be found in parts of Europe as an [[introduced species]] and a roadside [[weed]]. It is an extremely variable plant which is generally divided into many varieties, some of which may actually be specimens of other species.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250060798 Flora of North America]</ref>

==Description==
In general, it is a perennial herb producing a slender stem which is prostrate and spreading or erect, growing up to about 90 centimeters in maximum length. The leaves are up to about 13 centimeters long and can be most any shape. The [[inflorescence]] of this plant is an interrupted series of clusters of flowers. There are up to 20 flowers in each cluster, and each flower hangs from a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]. The flower usually has six [[tepal]]s, the inner three of which are largest and usually have central tubercles. It is an important food and host plant for ''[[Lycaena rubidus]]'' larvae.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Warren|first1=Andrew|last2=Harrera|first2=Alfonso|title=Butterflies of Oregon Their Taxonomy, Distribution, and Biology|url=https://dspace.library.colostate.edu/bitstream/handle/10217/81121/BSPMGILL_LepidopteraofNorthAmerica6.pdf?sequence=1|journal=Lepidoptera of North America}}</ref>
This plant usually is green colored with hints of pink and red.<ref>{{cite web |title=Willow Dock, Rumex Salicifolius |url=https://calscape.org/Rumex-salicifolius-() |website=Calscape}}</ref> It is also a Perennial plant, meaning that this plant usually lives for 2 or more years.

==Distribution==
''Rumex salicifolius'' is found in different parts of California, along with being found in Arizona, Nevada, and Northern Mexico. More recently it has been found as an introduced species in parts of Europe.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://beta.floranorthamerica.org/Rumex_salicifolius|title=Rumex salicifolius - FNA|website=beta.floranorthamerica.org|access-date=2019-11-06}}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Rumex salicifolius'' is typically found in wet places, but not flooded environments. These are areas adjacent to seasonally flooded wetlands, though. These plants can also be found on rocky slopes, and in margins. It is usually found less than 3,500{{specify|date=Octobe 2025}} altitude.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Severns |first1=Paul M. |title=Habitat restoration facilitates an ecological trap for a locally rare, wetland-restricted butterfly |journal=Insect Conservation and Diversity |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=184–191 |doi=10.1111/j.1752-4598.2010.00120.x |year=2011 |s2cid=84007008 }}</ref> The bloom period for this plant is June through September.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plant Characteristics and Associations |url=https://www.calflora.org/entry/plantchar.html?crn=7225 |website=Cal Flora}}</ref> The plant usually thrives in full sunlight, and only sometimes in partial shade.<ref>{{cite web |title=Willow dock, Rumex salicifolius |url=https://calscape.org/Rumex-salicifolius-() |website=Calscape}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==

It is a dicot, meaning that the plant has 2 embryonic leaves and/or cotyledons. It is of the kingdom Plantae, the order Caryophyllales, and the buckwheat family, Polygonaceae. The genus is ''Rumex'' L.- Dock<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=RUSA|title=Rumex salicifolius Weinm.|website=Rumex salicifolius}}</ref> There are also fifteen different subspecies. These are- ''Rumex salicifolius var. angustifolius, Rumex salicifolius var. angustivalvis, Rumex salicifolius var. crassus, Rumex salicifolius var. denticulatus, Rumex salicifolius fo. ecallosus, Rumex salicifolius var. lacustris, Rumex salicifolius subsp. mexicanus, Rumex salicifolius var. mexicanus, Rumex salicifolius var. montigenitus, Rumex salicifolius subsp. salicifolius, Rumex salicifolius fo. transitorius, Rumex salicifolius var. transitorius, Rumex salicifolius subsp. triangulivalvis, Rumex salicifolius var. triangulivalvis, and Rumex salicifolius var. utahensis.''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://tropicos.org/Name/26001448|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name - Rumex salicifolius var. triangulivalvis (Danser) J.C. Hickman|website=tropicos.org|access-date=2019-11-14}}</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Zuni people]] use the ''mexicanus'' variety medicinally. A strong [[infusion]] of the root is made and given to women by their husbands to help them to become pregnant.<ref>Stevenson, Matilda Coxe 1915 Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians. SI-BAE Annual Report #30 (p. 85)</ref> The ground root, or an infusion of it, is taken also for sore throat, especially by sword swallowers.<ref>Stevenson, p.59</ref> This species is also used in the treatment and management of chronic pain of the aboriginal people of the Canadian Boreal Forest. It is used to treat chronic migraine/headache, chronic back pain, and chronic rheumatism/arthritis. In studies it has proven to be successful in aiding people with anti-inflammation and significant pain relief.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Uprety|first1=Yadav|last2=Lacasse|first2=Anaïs|last3=Asselin|first3=Hugo|date=2016|title=Traditional Uses of Medicinal Plants from the Canadian Boreal Forest for the Management of Chronic Pain Syndromes|journal=Pain Practice|language=en|volume=16|issue=4|pages=459–466|doi=10.1111/papr.12284|pmid=25776550|s2cid=31135525|issn=1533-2500}}</ref>
